memory_update.text: DSGX should be tracked as a tariff-compliance software beneficiary, not a metals producer; exposure depends on customs filing, HTS classification, duty calculation, and global trade intelligence demand.
EXPD should be tracked as a customs brokerage/advisory capacity beneficiary from tariff volatility; verify durability through customs brokerage revenue and margins.
RS is a metals service-center and processing candidate for reshoring/tariff pass-through; exposure is broad but indirect and should be validated through gross margin, inventory, and customer mix.
CMC maps to domestic recycled long-steel capacity and explicitly cited Section 232 exemption elimination as a favorable backdrop for domestic long steel.
CENX has the strongest direct policy-to-capacity evidence among this pass due to U.S. primary aluminum smelter expansion and Mt. Holly restart/expansion announcements.

Critical minerals and pharma tariff exposures were not fully expanded in this pass because the strongest evidence found centered on metals, logistics compliance, and customs brokerage; a separate pass should examine MP, USAR, FCX, TECK, SCCO, ALB, LAC, and domestic API/CDMO candidates.

Tariff-driven beneficiaries and victims must be separated: domestic metals capacity and compliance services may benefit, while import-dependent downstream manufacturers may suffer unless pass-through, exemptions, or domestic sourcing are available.
